_scope_definitions.all: Any paper that declares a difference-in-differences / two-way-fixed-effects design: it states it compares the change in an outcome for a treated group against the change for a control/comparison group across time. Fires on the paper's own naming of the design (DiD, difference-in-differences, TWFE, event study around a treatment date). Does NOT fire for a pure cross-sectional comparison or a single-group before/after with no comparison group.
_scope_definitions.covariate_adjusted: Fires only when the paper states it conditions its DiD estimate on covariates: it adds control variables to the regression, matches on covariates, invokes conditional parallel trends, or reweights on a propensity score. Near-miss that does NOT fire: mentioning covariates only to describe the sample; including unit and time fixed effects alone (those define the base DiD, not covariate adjustment). If the paper never states it adjusts for covariates, the trigger is not fired and the gated check is NA.
_scope_definitions.staggered_timing: Fires only when the paper states that its treated units begin treatment at different times (words the paper uses: staggered adoption, differential/variable treatment timing, rollout, cohorts first treated in different periods). Near-miss that does NOT fire: the paper states all treated units are treated at one common date (single-onset / block design); a two-period two-group design; or an event study built around one shared adoption date. If the paper never describes its own timing as varying across units, the trigger is not fired and the gated check is NA.
_scope_definitions.fuzzy_did: Fires only when the paper states its treatment is not a sharp 0/1 switch that all treated units share: it describes a fuzzy design, a treatment rate/intensity/dose that changes partially, a continuous or ordered or multi-valued treatment, or heterogeneous-adoption exposure. Near-miss that does NOT fire: a sharp binary treatment that some units switch on at different dates (that is staggered_timing, not fuzzy); describing treatment 'intensity' only in prose while estimating a binary indicator. If the paper never describes a non-sharp treatment, the trigger is not fired and the gated check is NA.
_scope_definitions.few_treated_clusters: Fires only when the paper states that a small number of units (or clusters) are treated or change treatment status — e.g. it reports one, or a handful of, treated states/regions/firms, or says few units switch. Near-miss that does NOT fire: a large treated group described with clustered standard errors; many treated units clustered into a few groups for inference only. If the paper does not state that few units are treated, the trigger is not fired and the gated check is NA.
_scope_definitions.repeated_cross_sections: Fires only when the paper states its data are repeated cross-sections — a fresh sample of individuals drawn each period rather than the same units followed over time. Near-miss that does NOT fire: a balanced or unbalanced panel of the same units; pooled panel data. If the paper does not describe its data as repeated cross-sections, the trigger is not fired and the gated check is NA.

claim: Identifying the treatment effect requires that units are not affected by the treatment before it takes effect; without a no-anticipation condition the pre-treatment periods cannot serve as valid reference periods.
observable: Whether the paper states a no-anticipation assumption (or defines an anticipation horizon it will allow) for its treated units.
pass_condition: The paper states that treatment has no effect before its onset, or explicitly specifies and defends an anticipation window it permits.
flag_condition: The paper estimates a DiD effect without stating any no-anticipation assumption or anticipation horizon.
severity_basis: Sources state no-anticipation is necessary for DiD identification because treated units otherwise have no valid reference periods (Borusyak 2024 L61; Roth 2023 L80).
requirement_statement: A DiD paper must state a no-anticipation assumption (or the anticipation horizon it allows).

evidence.quote: the no-anticipation assumption, which states that the treatment has no causal effect prior to its implementation
some form of this assumption is necessary for DiD identification, as there would be no reference periods for treated units otherwise.

claim: The potential-outcomes framework underlying DiD assumes one unit's outcomes do not depend on other units' treatment (SUTVA / no interference), which rules out spillovers and general-equilibrium effects.
observable: Whether the paper acknowledges the no-interference / no-spillover (SUTVA) assumption, or discusses whether treatment of some units could affect the outcomes of others.
pass_condition: The paper states the no-interference / SUTVA assumption, or explicitly discusses whether spillovers between treated and comparison units could contaminate the estimate.
flag_condition: The paper estimates a DiD effect without acknowledging the no-interference / no-spillover assumption at all.
severity_basis: Sources state that a SUTVA violation means neither potential outcome is observed, invalidating the DiD estimate (Baker 2022 L56; Roth 2023 L61).
requirement_statement: A DiD paper must acknowledge the no-interference / no-spillover (SUTVA) assumption its estimate relies on.

claim: Covariates used to make parallel trends more credible must be measured before treatment and unaffected by it; conditioning on a covariate that the treatment itself can move induces bad-control (post-treatment) bias.
observable: For a paper that conditions on covariates, whether any control it uses is measured or realized after treatment onset (or is itself a plausible outcome of the treatment).
pass_condition: The controls the paper conditions on are pre-treatment (measured before onset) or otherwise argued to be unaffected by the treatment.
flag_condition: The paper conditions its estimate on at least one covariate measured after treatment onset, or on a variable it acknowledges the treatment can affect, without treating that as a limitation.
severity_basis: Sources require conditioning covariates to be pre-treatment and unaffected by treatment (Roth 2023 L322; Callaway 2020 L476-478; Borusyak 2024 L59); conditioning on affected covariates biases the ATT.
requirement_statement: A covariate-adjusted DiD must not condition on covariates measured after treatment onset or affected by the treatment.

claim: Conditional-on-covariates DiD additionally requires an overlap (positivity) condition: for the covariate values present, both treated and comparison units must exist so the comparison group can stand in for the treated group.
observable: For a paper conditioning on covariates, whether it reports or discusses common support / overlap of covariates between treated and comparison units (e.g. propensity scores bounded away from 0/1, a support/trimming discussion, a balance table over the conditioning set).

flag_condition: The paper conditions on covariates for identification but reports no evidence or discussion of overlap / common support between treated and comparison units.
severity_basis: Sources impose overlap/positivity as a required condition for conditional DiD and note it is particularly important for valid inference (Roth 2023 L251; Callaway 2020 L308-312; Sant’Anna 2020 L172).
requirement_statement: A covariate-adjusted DiD should report or discuss overlap (positivity) of the conditioning covariates across treated and comparison units.

claim: When treatment timing is staggered and treatment effects vary across groups or over time, a single-coefficient or dynamic two-way-fixed-effects regression is biased for the average effect, because already-treated units serve as controls and some group-time effects receive negative weights. Papers with staggered timing must therefore either use a heterogeneity-robust estimator or state an ex-ante justification for restricting effect heterogeneity.
observable: For a paper that declares staggered timing, whether its main effect estimate comes from a heterogeneity-robust estimator (e.g. one that only compares newly-treated to not-yet-/never-treated units) OR is accompanied by a stated theoretical justification for assuming homogeneous effects.
pass_condition: The paper reports a heterogeneity-robust estimate for its staggered design (a group-time / imputation / stacked / not-yet-treated-control estimator), or plain TWFE accompanied by an explicit ex-ante argument that treatment effects are homogeneous across groups and time.
flag_condition: The paper's staggered-timing effect rests on a single-coefficient or dynamic TWFE regression with no heterogeneity-robust estimate reported and no stated justification for a homogeneity restriction.
severity_basis: Sources show staggered TWFE can be wrong-signed relative to every underlying effect (Goodman-Bacon 2021 L69; Roth 2023 L143; Baker 2022 L119; Chaisemartin 2022 L7), so an unaddressed staggered TWFE estimate can reverse the reported conclusion.
prevalence_aggravator: Several sources note the bias grows with the spread of adoption dates and shrinks with the share of never-treated units, so it is most severe in designs with wide timing variation and few never-treated units.
requirement_statement: A staggered-timing DiD must report a heterogeneity-robust estimate or state an ex-ante justification for assuming homogeneous treatment effects.

evidence.quote: the combination of stag- gered treatment timing and treatment effect heterogeneity, either across groups or over time, leads to biased TWFE
treatment effects vary over time, in which case it typically biases regression DD estimates away
We show that conventional regression-based estimators fail to provide unbiased estimates of relevant estimands absent strong restrictions on treatment-effect homogeneity.

claim: Units already treated before the first observed period have no observed untreated baseline, so they cannot identify a treatment effect nor serve as a valid comparison group; a paper must not retain them as treated or control units as if that baseline existed.
observable: Whether the paper affirmatively retains units already treated before the first observed period as treated or comparison units as if their untreated baseline were observed.
pass_condition: The paper does not retain units already treated before the first observed period as treated or comparison units. Designs with no such units comply; undisclosed pre-window treatment status defaults to PASS.
flag_condition: The paper affirmatively retains units already treated before the first observed period as treated or control units, with no note that their untreated outcomes are never observed.
severity_basis: Callaway (2020) shows treatment effects are unidentified for units treated before the first period, and they are invalid as a comparison group.
requirement_statement: Units already treated before the first observed period have no observed untreated baseline, so they cannot identify a treatment effect nor serve as a valid comparison group; a paper must not retain them as treated or control units as if that baseline existed.

evidence.quote: untreated potential outcomes are never observed for this group which will imply that treatment effects are not identified for this group nor are they useful as a comparison group under a parallel trends assumption.

claim: For a non-sharp (fuzzy / continuous / heterogeneous-adoption) treatment, the Wald-DiD ratio identifies a causal effect only under extra treatment-effect homogeneity assumptions, and assumption-free fuzzy estimands require a control group whose treatment exposure is stable over time; a fuzzy-design paper must state which of these it relies on.
observable: For a paper that declares a non-sharp treatment, whether it states the additional assumption its fuzzy/continuous estimand needs — either a treatment-effect homogeneity condition or a control group with stable treatment exposure across periods.
pass_condition: The paper states the homogeneity assumption behind its Wald-DiD estimate, or identifies a control group whose treatment exposure is stable over time for an assumption-free fuzzy estimand.
flag_condition: The paper estimates a fuzzy / continuous / heterogeneous-adoption DiD effect without stating either the required treatment-effect homogeneity assumption or a stable-exposure control group.
severity_basis: Sources show the Wald-DiD identifies a LATE only if homogeneity assumptions hold and can otherwise reverse sign (Chaisemartin 2017 L2, L72, L74); assumption-free estimands need a stable-exposure control group (Chaisemartin 2017 L23).
requirement_statement: A fuzzy / continuous-treatment DiD must state the treatment-effect homogeneity assumption behind its Wald-DiD estimate or identify a stable-exposure control group.

evidence.quote: We show that this ratio identifies a local average treatment effect only if two homogeneous treatment effect assumptions are satisfied

claim: DiD outcomes are typically serially correlated and treatment status changes little within a group over time, so treating observations as independent understates the standard errors and over-rejects the null; inference must account for within-group serial correlation and clustering.
observable: Whether the paper's reported inference accounts for within-group correlation — e.g. standard errors clustered at the group level, a block bootstrap, aggregation to pre/post, or another serial-correlation-robust procedure — rather than assuming independent errors.
pass_condition: The paper reports standard errors that account for within-group serial correlation and clustering (cluster-robust at the assignment level, block bootstrap, pre/post aggregation, or an equivalent serial-correlation-robust method).
flag_condition: The paper reports conventional/independent-observation standard errors (or does not describe how it handles serial correlation and clustering) for a multi-period DiD.
severity_basis: Sources find conventional DiD standard errors reject a false null in up to 45% of placebo runs (Bertrand 2004 L3) and that ignoring grouped errors yields inconsistent standard errors (Bertrand 2004 L17; Wing 2018 L96).
requirement_statement: A multi-period DiD must report inference that accounts for within-group serial correlation and clustering.

evidence.quote: These conventional DD standard errors severely understate the standard deviation of the estimators: we find an “effect” significant at the 5 percent level for up to 45 percent of the placebo interventions.
Ignoring this grouped data problem can lead to inconsistent standard errors.

claim: When only a small number of units are treated or change treatment status, large-sample cluster-robust inference is unreliable — it understates uncertainty and over-rejects — and a small-cluster-appropriate procedure is needed instead.
observable: For a paper that states it has few treated units/clusters, whether it uses an inference method suited to that case (randomization/permutation or Conley-Taber-type inference, pre/post aggregation with a small-sample-adjusted threshold, a wild-cluster bootstrap with stated caveats, or reported wider intervals) rather than routine large-sample cluster-robust standard errors.
pass_condition: The paper uses a small-cluster-appropriate inference procedure for its few treated units (randomization/permutation, Conley-Taber, aggregated inference with adjusted critical values, or an explicitly caveated wild bootstrap).
flag_condition: The paper has few treated units/clusters yet reports only routine large-sample cluster-robust standard errors, with no small-sample adjustment or alternative method.
severity_basis: Sources state cluster-robust standard errors are very misleading with few changers (Conley 2010 L252), the cluster CLT is a poor approximation with few treated clusters (Roth 2023 L401), and the bias worsens for the near-constant treatment variables typical of DiD (Bertrand 2004 L219).
requirement_statement: A DiD with few treated units/clusters must use inference designed for the small-cluster case rather than routine large-sample cluster-robust standard errors.

evidence.quote: cluster standard errors can be very misleading when the number of groups changing status is small.

claim: Because parallel trends is untestable and pre-trends tests can miss meaningful violations, conventional confidence intervals can badly undercover; a credible DiD should probe how sensitive its conclusion is to plausible violations of parallel trends.
observable: Whether the paper reports at least one item from an enumerated set of parallel-trends robustness artifacts: (a) a formal parallel-trends sensitivity analysis or robust confidence set (e.g. one that bounds the post-treatment trend violation by the pre-treatment violation); (b) a placebo or pre-period test aimed at detecting trend violations; (c) estimates under at least one alternative comparison/control group; or (d) estimates under at least one alternative specification that the paper presents as a check on the trend assumption. Presence of any one item is readable from the paper's tables, figures, or text.
pass_condition: The paper reports at least one of the enumerated artifacts (a)–(d).
flag_condition: The paper reports its DiD estimate and none of the enumerated artifacts (a)–(d) appears anywhere in the paper, appendix, or supplement.
severity_basis: Sources state that underpowered pre-trends tests can leave conventional confidence intervals severely undercovering the true effect (Rambachan 2023 L40), motivating inference and reporting that account for possible trend violations; Roth 2023 (Table 1, L37) lists formal sensitivity analyses among recommended DiD reporting steps.
requirement_statement: A DiD paper should report at least one of the enumerated parallel-trends robustness artifacts (formal sensitivity analysis / robust confidence set, placebo or pre-period test, alternative comparison group, or a trend-robustness specification check).

evidence.quote: pre-trends tests may be underpowered against meaningful violations of parallel trends, potentially leading to severe undercoverage of conventional confidence intervals

claim: Parallel pre-treatment trends do not prove that parallel trends holds after treatment, pre-trends tests often have low power, and conditioning the analysis on passing a pre-trends test induces pre-test selection bias; a paper must not treat a passed pre-trends test as proof of identification or filter its analysis on that test.
observable: Whether the paper (a) claims that observing parallel pre-trends establishes the parallel-trends assumption, or (b) states it selected its sample, specification, or decision to proceed on the basis of passing a pre-trends test.
pass_condition: The paper does not treat parallel pre-trends as proof of the assumption and does not condition its analysis on passing a pre-trends test (silence about pre-testing counts as compliance here).
flag_condition: The paper asserts that parallel pre-trends establish the parallel-trends assumption, or states it retained/dropped the design or filtered results based on the outcome of a pre-trends test.
severity_basis: Sources state pre-trends tests may fail to reject owing to low power (Roth 2023 L344) and that conditioning on passing them induces pre-test bias (Roth 2023 L348); parallel trends itself is not directly testable (Baker 2022 L154).
requirement_statement: A DiD paper must not treat passed pre-trends as proof of parallel trends, nor condition its analysis on the outcome of a pre-trends test.

evidence.quote: the tests described above may fail to reject owing to low power

claim: Under staggered timing with heterogeneous effects, the lead coefficients of a two-way-fixed-effects event study are contaminated by the treatment effects of other periods and cohorts, so they are not a valid test of pre-trends; a staggered-design paper must not rely on TWFE event-study leads as its pre-trends test.
observable: For a paper that declares staggered timing, whether the pre-trends evidence it relies on comes from the lead coefficients of a plain TWFE event-study regression, rather than from a heterogeneity-robust pre-trends test (leads from a robust group-time/imputation estimator, or a test run on untreated observations only).
pass_condition: The paper either uses a heterogeneity-robust pre-trends test for its staggered design, or does not present TWFE event-study lead coefficients as evidence for parallel trends.
flag_condition: The paper relies on the lead coefficients of a plain TWFE event-study regression as its pre-trends test in a staggered-timing design.
severity_basis: Sources show TWFE event-study leads can be nonzero even when parallel trends holds and are contaminated across cohorts, making pre-trend evaluation from them misleading (Roth 2023 L174; Baker 2022 L174; Chaisemartin 2022 L149).
requirement_statement: A staggered-timing DiD must not use plain TWFE event-study lead coefficients as its test of pre-trends.

author_guidance: State the target estimand you are after (e.g. the ATT, or an event-study path of effects) and which units and periods identify it — the comparison group and the time frame. Making the estimand and the identifying comparison explicit, rather than letting a regression specification implicitly impose them, lets a reader see what your coefficient represents.
claim: A central source of DiD estimation problems is imposing an estimand implicitly through a regression specification instead of naming the target parameter and the comparison groups that identify it; papers should make the estimand and comparison explicit.
observable: Whether the paper states its target estimand (e.g. the ATT or an event-study path) and identifies the comparison group(s) and time frame used to identify it.
pass_condition: The paper names its target estimand and identifies the comparison group(s) and time frame that identify it.
flag_condition: The paper reports a DiD coefficient without stating the estimand it targets or the comparison group(s) identifying it.
severity_basis: Sources identify imposing implicit homogeneity instead of specifying a target estimand as a central danger (Borusyak 2024 L23) and recommend transparency about the estimand and comparison groups (Roth 2023 L43).
requirement_statement: A DiD paper should state its target estimand and the comparison groups and time frame that identify it.

claim: With repeated cross-sections, identification requires that the joint distribution of group membership and covariates be stable across periods; unaddressed compositional change across periods biases the estimate.
observable: For a paper stating it uses repeated cross-sections, whether it addresses the stability of group composition and covariate distribution across periods (states the stable-composition assumption, or reports evidence that composition does not shift with treatment).
pass_condition: The paper states or examines that group membership and the covariate distribution are stable across periods (no compositional change confounding the comparison).
flag_condition: The paper uses repeated cross-sections but never addresses whether group composition or the covariate distribution shifts across periods.
severity_basis: Sources state repeated-cross-section identification rules out compositional changes over time (Callaway 2020 L1653-1654; Sant’Anna 2020 L160) and that stability of group membership is required (Chaisemartin 2017 L170).
requirement_statement: A repeated-cross-section DiD must address the stability of group composition and covariate distribution across periods.
